description: We are Team ZenoX from India: Bhagnesh Karmuk Raghav (Systems & Astropy Pipeline), Kshitij Vats (Spectral Analysis & IRSA APIs), Yuvika Rathore (Cosmic UI & JS9 Visualization), and Tanisha Shrivastava (Time-Domain Research & Guides). United by a passion for open science, we combined Python astrophysics and interactive web design to build ZenoX:SpherexView—making NASA's 102-band infrared sky accessible to all.
summary:
ZenoX:SpherexView is an interactive, browser-based time-lapse and spectral sky workbench developed by Team ZenoX that transforms NASA’s SPHEREx archive into an accessible discovery tool. While SPHEREx maps the entire sky across 102 infrared channels (0.75–5.00 µm) every six months, hunting for moving objects or variable stars traditionally requires writing complex Python scripts and downloading massive Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) files from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).
Our platform addresses the challenge by automating live IRSA spatial queries (TAP/SIA v2), slicing calibrated cutouts with Astropy WCS-WAVE spectrophotometry, and pairing WiseView-style Asinh brightness stretching with an embedded Harvard-Smithsonian JS9 WebAssembly FITS engine. Users can animate chronological epochs at 1–12 FPS, enable Difference Mode (Epoch − Median) to erase static stars so moving brown dwarfs and Planet X candidates pop out, and compare all six infrared detector bands (D1–D6) side-by-side. By combining zero-install access with built-in plain-English ⓘ guides, ZenoX:SpherexView democratizes infrared time-domain astronomy for researchers, students, and citizen scientists worldwide.
details:
Here is a comprehensive, judge-ready response for the "Project Details" section of your 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge submission form. You can copy and paste this directly into the submission portal:

Project Details: ZenoX:SpherexView

Team Name: Team ZenoX (Bhagnesh Karmuk Raghav, Kshitij Vats, Yuvika Rathore, Tanisha Shrivastava)
Challenge: Planet X and SPHEREx
Live Deployment: https://zenox-spherexview.vercel.app

1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

ZenoX:SpherexView is an interactive, full-stack astronomical time-lapse and spectral sky workbench designed to unlock NASA’s SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) archive for both professional researchers and citizen scientists.

While SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months across 102 near- to mid-infrared spectral channels (0.75–5.00 µm) using six Linear Variable Filter (LVF) detector arrays (D1–D6), inspecting an object across time currently requires writing custom Virtual Observatory (pyvo) queries, downloading large Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) files from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), and manually resolving 2D tabular wavelength headers (WCS-WAVE). ZenoX:SpherexView automates this entire scientific workflow inside a zero-install web browser through a 4-Stage Pipeline:

  1. Stage 1 — Smart ICRS Coordinate & Target Resolution (Where?):
    • Users enter any sky coordinates in sexagesimal (16h32m42.34s +66d45m22.7s) or decimal degrees (248.1764 66.7563), type an object name, or select a one-click benchmark target (R Draconis, Cat’s Eye Nebula, Pinwheel Galaxy M101, SPHEREx NEP Deep Field, Cygnus Benchmark Star, or Barnard’s Star).
    • Our Python FastAPI microservice parses and validates the coordinates onto the international ICRS J2000 celestial grid using astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord.
    • Tier 1 (Live NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA v2 & CAOM TAP): The backend queries Caltech’s official SPHEREx collections (spherex_dr1, spherex_dr1_deep, spherex_qr3) via IVOA Simple Image Access v2 (SIA) and executes spatial polygon ADQL queries (CONTAINS(POINT('ICRS', ra, dec), p.poly)) joining spherex.artifact and spherex.plane on https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/TAP.
    • Tier 2 (Real-Sky Multi-Survey Infrared Failover): If Caltech’s primary server is undergoing scheduled maintenance or experiences network timeouts, the engine automatically fails over within 3.5 seconds to Lawrence Berkeley National Lab’s Legacy Survey / unWISE FITS cutout service (unwise-neo7 W1 3.4 µm & W2 4.6 µm, ls-dr10 z-band 0.92 µm) and CDS HiPS2FITS (2MASS J/H/Ks 1.23–2.16 µm) to retrieve real calibrated infrared FITS cutouts at the exact requested (RA, Dec) and Field of View (FOV).
    • Tier 3 (Orbital Visibility Schedule & Caching): Computes authentic sun-synchronous orbital visit counts (16 visits near the North Ecliptic Pole at +66.56°, 9–12 visits at mid-latitudes, 6 visits near the equator) and Modified Julian Date (MJD) baselines, caching raw NumPy arrays in RAM.
    • For every exposure, astropy.io.fits extracts the 2D science array (IMAGE HDU) and crops it to the user’s requested arcsecond Field of View (Cutout2D) at SPHEREx’s native 6.15"/pixel scale.
    • It evaluates SPHEREx’s alternate tabular spectral coordinate system (WCS(header, fobj=hdul, key="W")) at the target’s pixel position (X, Y) to compute the exact central infrared wavelength (
      λλ
      in
      μmμm
      ).
    • It measures background-subtracted Aperture Flux inside a central 5×5 pixel aperture after subtracting the median zodiacal sky glow (Min, Med, Max in MJy/sr).
    • It normalizes pixel values using finite-pixel statistics (JS9 Min/Max, Adapt MAD σ adaptive sky-noise clipping, or Percent clipping) and applies an Inverse Hyperbolic Sine (AsinhStretch) curve—boosting faint brown dwarfs and nebulae without saturating bright star cores.
    • Animated Blink Comparator (1–12 FPS): Flips chronologically through epochs so stationary background stars remain fixed while moving objects (proper-motion stars, Planet X candidates, asteroids) jump across the reticle and variable stars pulse.
    • Difference Mode (Epoch − Median): Subtracts the per-band median reference image (np.nanmedian) from each frame so static stars cancel out to zero, isolating transient and moving sources.
    • Synchronized 6-Band Strip (D1–D6): Displays all chronological visits and spectral channels (0.75–5.00 µm) side by side under identical stretch and zoom settings.
    • Embedded Harvard-Smithsonian JS9 WebAssembly Engine: With one click, users can switch into the official JS9 FITS Viewer running in WebAssembly (astroemw.wasm) to inspect the raw single-HDU .fits file directly in the browser.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Zero-Install, Cross-Device Accessibility: Runs entirely in any desktop or mobile phone web browser—eliminating the need to install Python environments, download multi-hundred-megabyte raw MEF files, or write ADQL/Astropy scripts.
  • Sub-50ms Real-Time Photometric Re-Stretching: Because raw 2D NumPy FITS arrays are cached in FastAPI memory by session_id, dragging the Asinh Softening (a), Trim Bright (%), Scaling Mode, Colormap LUT (Magma, Viridis, Grayscale, Cividis), or Invert Polarity controls updates all epoch frames in under 50 milliseconds without re-querying NASA’s servers.
  • Simultaneous Time + Wavelength Inspection: Unlike traditional viewers that only show a single broadband filter, ZenoX:SpherexView lets users track how an object behaves across both time (MJD epochs) and wavelength (0.75–5.00 µm)—for example, watching a cold Y-dwarf remain invisible in D1/D2 (0.9–1.4 µm) and suddenly blaze into view in thermal bands D5/D6 (4.1–4.7 µm).
  • Touch & Mouse Live WCS Sky Coordinate Probe: Moving a mouse cursor (or dragging a finger on a phone screen) across any cutout calculates real-time celestial ICRS RA / Dec coordinates from the FITS World Coordinate System (WCS) matrix.
  • Built-In Plain-English Education (ⓘ System): Every single section and technical control has a clickable ⓘ Info Icon and a Beginner’s Glossary Modal written in clear, everyday language so high-school students and newcomers can learn infrared astronomy while using professional-grade tools.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

  1. Accelerating Citizen Science & Moving-Object Discovery:
    Inspired by the success of WiseView and the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project, ZenoX:SpherexView gives citizen scientists a dedicated blink-and-difference workbench for SPHEREx’s 102-channel survey—helping uncover太陽-neighborhood brown dwarfs, distant outer-solar-system bodies (Planet X candidates), and extreme infrared variable stars.
  2. Empowering STEM Classrooms & Universities:
    Students can visually explore how SPHEREx’s polar sun-synchronous orbit creates deep fields at the North and South Ecliptic Poles, how different infrared wavelengths reveal specific molecules (Paschen-α at 1.87 µm, water ice at 3.05 µm, PAH organic dust at 3.3 µm, and CO₂/CO ice at 4.27–4.67 µm), and verify their findings by downloading raw NASA .fits files with one click.
  3. Providing Reproducible Open Science:
    Every query exposes the exact executed IRSA TAP ADQL query and direct FITS cutout URLs, allowing researchers to copy the SQL query directly into their own papers, notebooks, or Virtual Observatory tools (such as TOPCAT or DS9).

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Programming Languages:
    • Python 3.11 / 3.14 (Backend scientific computing, FITS/WCS processing, and Virtual Observatory queries)
    • TypeScript & JavaScript (ES2022) (Frontend state management, WCS cursor math, and Express gateway)
    • ADQL / SQL (Astronomical Data Query Language for spatial polygon queries on IRSA CAOM tables)
    • HTML5, CSS3 & SVG (Responsive layout, custom interactive orbital globes, and spectral rulers)
    • Astropy (astropy.io.fits, astropy.wcs, astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord, astropy.nddata.Cutout2D, astropy.time.Time, astropy.visualization.AsinhStretch): Authoritative FITS HDU parsing, WCS-WAVE lookup, spatial slicing, aperture photometry, and non-linear stretching.
    • pyvo: IVOA Virtual Observatory client for TAP and SIA v2 service discovery.
    • NumPy & Pillow (PIL): High-speed 2D matrix math, per-band median reference subtraction (np.nanmedian), MAD
      σσ
      noise estimation, RGB LUT interpolation, and lossless PNG encoding.
    • FastAPI & Pydantic: High-performance Python REST API with strict schema validation and JSON NaN/Inf sanitization.
    • Node.js & Express: API gateway, uvicorn process supervisor, and same-origin proxy for JS9 WebAssembly workers.
    • React 19 & Vite 6: Reactive UI with debounced photometric re-rendering and keyboard/touch navigation.
    • Tailwind CSS v4 & Lucide React: Custom cosmic observatory design system and iconography.
    • Harvard-Smithsonian JS9 (WebAssembly / astroemw.wasm): Embedded in-browser FITS engine for interactive contrast/bias manipulation and header analysis.
    • NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): spherex.plane, spherex.artifact, spherex_dr1, spherex_dr1_deep, and spherex_qr3.
    • LBNL Legacy Survey (unWISE Neo7 / DESI ls-dr10) & CDS HiPS2FITS (2MASS): Multi-survey infrared FITS failover archives.
    • Vercel & Docker: Serverless Python + static edge deployment (https://zenox-spherexview.vercel.app) and containerized local/cloud runtime.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

  1. Bridging Story-Driven Visual Education with a Live Research Workbench:
    Most astronomy tools are either oversimplified static websites with no real data, or intimidating command-line/FITS interfaces with a steep learning curve. ZenoX:SpherexView unites both worlds: users are guided through Where? When? What changed?, an interactive 3D Celestial Survey Globe, and a 102-Color Infrared Spectrum Ruler, which feed directly into a live, research-grade FITS blink and spectrophotometry console.
  2. Dual Rendering Engine (Fast Flipbook Blinking + Live JS9 WebAssembly):
    Blinking 16 raw FITS files at 12 FPS in JavaScript alone can lag on mobile devices, while static PNGs lack deep FITS header inspection. We solved this creatively by pairing server-side Astropy Asinh PNG buffering (for instant 12 FPS blinking and 16-card strip comparison) with an on-demand single-HDU FITS builder that streams the active epoch into Harvard’s JS9 WebAssembly engine.
  3. 3-Tier Self-Healing Archive Failover:
    Live astronomical databases periodically undergo maintenance windows (such as Caltech IPAC’s Sunday morning server maintenance). Rather than failing with an error screen, our 3-tier client detects upstream 502 Proxy Errors within 3.5 seconds and seamlessly synthesizes multi-band infrared FITS cutouts from complementary NASA/CDS sky surveys (unWISE & 2MASS) matched to SPHEREx’s 0.75–5.00 µm bandpasses and orbital cadence.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • SPHEREx Orbital Mechanics & Cadence: Because SPHEREx orbits Earth pole-to-pole every 98 minutes in a sun-synchronous orbit, sky coverage is not uniform—targets near the North and South Ecliptic Poles (±66.56°, such as R Draconis and the Cat’s Eye Nebula) receive dozens of visits, while equatorial targets (Barnard’s Star) are visited in sparser 6-month passes. We curated our benchmark catalog and orbital scheduler to reflect this real physical geometry.
  • Infrared Detector Dynamic Range & Zodiacal Background: In bands D4–D6 (2.4–5.0 µm), thermal glow from interplanetary zodiacal dust creates a bright background pedestal (~15–40 MJy/sr). Standard linear scaling washes out the image into a white square. We specifically implemented Median Absolute Deviation (Adapt MAD σ) and JS9 Min/Max Asinh scaling on strictly finite pixels (np.isfinite) so stars and nebulae stand out sharply against the zodiacal background.
  • JSON Compliance with Astronomical NaN Pixels: Cropped FITS cutouts frequently contain NaN (Not-a-Number) padding at rotated detector edges or in distorted WCS polynomial regions, which crashes standard REST JSON serializers. We engineered recursive safe_float() and sanitize_json() guards across the pipeline.
  • Universal Mobile & Classroom Usability: Not every student has a desktop workstation. We designed touch-screen WCS coordinate probing (onTouchMove), responsive mobile navigation drawers, and a built-in widescreen pitch deck (presentation.html) so the entire platform works seamlessly on smartphones, tablets, and laptops.

How NASA Data & Resources Were Used:
ZenoX:SpherexView queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) via its TAP (spherex.plane

⋈⋈

spherex.artifact) and SIA v2 (spherex_dr1, spherex_dr1_deep, spherex_qr3) APIs to discover multi-epoch SPHEREx Level 2 Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) exposures across all six infrared detector bands (D1–D6, 0.75–5.00 µm). Following Caltech/IPAC’s official SPHEREx cutout and WCS-WAVE methodology, our backend extracts calibrated 6.15"/px spatial cutouts, evaluates exact pixel wavelengths, and applies NASA Backyard Worlds (WiseView) Asinh photometric stretching and median difference imaging. We also integrate the Harvard-Smithsonian / NASA JS9 WebAssembly FITS engine for in-browser FITS HDU analysis and use NASA WISE (unWISE) and 2MASS infrared FITS archives for resilient all-sky failover.
